biography: In the 1891 census she is found at Ripple Lodge, Malvern Link with her younger sister Margaret.
In 1891 cook to CMY at Elderfield;  in 1861, 1871 and 1901 working for the ‘Indian Moberlys’.

Daughter of Sir Charles Thomas Palmer, 2nd Bt., she married (17 January 1850) the Rt. Rev. Charles John Abraham (1814-1903).  She and Sarah Harriet (Richardson) Selwyn were first cousins. Her sister Mary Anne Palmer was living in 1871 near Mary Anne Dyson at Ewshott in Hants.

description: 1st Bishop of Wellington, New Zealand, and later Suffragan Bishop of Derby
biography: He married (1850) Caroline Harriet Palmer (1809/10-1877)[ODNB, WWW]
Eldest of the six daughters of Arthur Acland Troyte, sister of Joanna (Acland Troyte) Harper, who was a Gosling as ‘Albatross’, she married (1863) the Rev. Charles Sandford Bere (d. 1889).
Father of Frances and Joanna Acland Troyte and four other daughters,  brother of Sir Thomas Dyke Acland, 11th Bt. (1809–1898).  He changed his surname to Acland Troyte.
Brother of Arthur Acland Troyte and of Sir Thomas Dyke Acland. [ODNB]

description: photographer, daughter of Sir Henry Wentworth Acland
politician and educationist, father of Agnes (Acland) Anson and brother of Arthur Acland Troyte and Sir Henry Wentworth Acland
evidently a humble Devon friend of WCY
probably a parishioner of the Rev. Richard Carter Smith in Woolwich

biography: He married, first (1861), Georgina Alethe Polson (b.1838), daughter of the Rev. Hugh Polson and Georgiana, only child of Charlotte Yonge and her first husband Captain George Crawley, and therefore CMY’s first cousin once removed.  (Mrs Crawley was CMY's aunt and godmother and married secondly the Rev Thomas Jones, Rector of Exeter College Oxford). The Polsons had other children: (Arthur b. 1831/2, George b. 1833/4, Rosalia b.1834/5 and Catharina K. b. 1835/6). Adams married secondly (24 June 1885), in the teeth of her family, the Hon. Mildred Mary Coleridge (1847-14 January 1929). For his involvement in brawling during a church service at St. George in the East, in defence of the innovations introduced by the vicar, see The Times (11, 14 April 1860). [LG 1952 Woollcombe Adams of Anstey Hall; 1841, 1851, 1861 censuses at www.ancestry.co.uk]

description: first cousin once removed to CMY, first wife of Charles Warren Adams
biography: The Times (11 January 1862) reported the marriage 'at Cape-town, cape of good Hope, Charles Warren Adams, Esq, son of the late Mr. Serjeant Adams to Georgiana Alethe, youngest daughter of the Rev. Hugh Polson.' The death of a Georgiana Alethe Adams aged 2 was registered in Fulham in 1880. According to the Bristol Mercury and Daily Post (24 November 1884) Charles Warren Adams stated in court that he had lived happily with his wife who had died of cancer. He had always supported his daughter. The refusal of the Bishop of Cape Town to marry them was a mistake, and he had afterwards been reconciled to her family.

Birth registered Westminster 11 August 1862 of Charlotte Alethe Rosalie Adams, daughter of Georgiana Alsthe Adams and Charles Warren Adams.  Charlotte A. R. Adams is boarder in New Shoreham west Sussex in the 1891 census; visiting an old lady in Brighton in 1901.
Mary Adams lived in Otterbourne 1862-71 and ran a small boarding school with her aunt Mary La Beaune (b. Middlesex 1820/1)

description: American journalist and writer, contributor to MP
member of the Gosling Society as ‘Ladybird’
biography: The only daughter of John Duke Coleridge, later 1st Lord Coleridge, and Jane Fortescue Seymour (d. 1878), she married (24 June 1885) Charles Warren Adams. She had a row with her father about her marriage which was made public because Adams sued her brother Bernard for libel.  She was a Gosling as Ladybird 1859- c. 1866;   [PB, Coleridge, Story of a Devonshire House; The Times reports of the libel trial 21, 22 November 1884, 5, 25 June 1885.]
Briefly engaged to the Hon. Jane Colborne in 1845, he later married (20 August 1846) Lady Louisa Noel (d.1883). [PB]
Her address was 39 Green Street Grosvenor Square.  Her paper on \'The Ladies Home\' describes her as its Hon. Secretary.  She is found there living with her younger brother in the 1871 census.
Perhaps Mary Anne (Berthon) Alderson, wife of the physician Sir James Alderson (1794-1882), Kt. 1869, and sister of the Rev. Edward Berthon, vicar of Romsey.
An early friend of CMY, she married (15 October 1850) the Rt. Rev. William Alexander (1824-1911), Dean of Emly (1864) Bishop of Derry (1867), later (1896) Archbishop of Armagh.
He served as Dean of Canterbury from 1857 to his death. He was associated with campaigns against ritualism, which may account for CMY\'s sense that he was not fully sympathetic to her.

description: member of the Gosling Society and contributor to MP
biography: Daughter of the Rev. John Collins Allen, Vicar of Hawley, Hants 1878-86, she was a Gosling as ‘Gridiron’. Living at Finchcox, Kilndown, Staplehurst (10 July 1870) and Hinton Martel Rectory, Wimborne (December 1876), she was perhaps a governess. She was author of 45 odd novels, stories for SPCK and translations. She was lame. [Vital Records Index; 1881 census, Will;  Alumni Oxonienses; Who\'s Who in Lit 1906-34; BL cat]
Son of the physicist André Marie Ampère (d. 1836).

The eldest daughter of the Rev. John Yonge of Puslinch and Alethea Henrietta Bargus, she married (1845) John Philip Anderson Morshead of Widey Court, her second cousin, whose paternal grandmother was Elizabeth Yonge of Puslinch.  They had six sons. She and her younger sister Anne were known as ‘great A and little a’, after a nursery rhyme.  [LG 1871 Morshead]

Always called Mary, she was the daughter of Pentire Anderson Morshead and Charlotte Story; her paternal grandmother was a Yonge which made her a cousin of CMY. She joined the Gosling Society as ‘Bog Oak’ and was one of the liveliest contributors to The Barnacle, she left when she went to South Africa to do missionary and social work in 1868; she later wrote a history of the Universities Mission to Central Africa 1859-1896 (1897) and  A Pioneer and Founder . . . Robert Gray, first Bishop of Cape Town (1905).  She  also edited Eikon Basilike (1887). For many years, from at least 1881, she was a matron at Marlborough St Giles Industrial School for Girls, Andover. Many of her contributions to MP are signed ‘Bog Oak’. Jackson’s Oxford Journal (30 May 1891) reports her speaking at a GFS conference as a member of the committee for the Winchester Diocese. She was first cousin to fellow-Goslings Mary Sunderland and Anne Baker.
He qualified MRCS from UCL in 1875. He was fifth son of the Rev. John Philip Anderson Morshead and Alethea Yonge. [LG 1871; Winchester College Register]
The second son of the Rev. John Philip Anderson Morshead and Alethea Yonge. [Winchester College Register]

description: cousin of CMY, sister of Mary Anderson Morshead
biography: Known as Beatrice, a member of the Gosling Society as ‘Queen Bee’, she married (1880)  her cousin John Yonge Anderson Morshead (1846-1923), barrister. They lived at Salcombe. At the time of the 1871 census she was a pupil at Mary Anne Dyson’s school at Crondall. [1861, 71 census]
Son of Captain Pentyre Anderson Morshead and  brother of Mary Anderson Morshead [1861 census]

Eldest son of the Rev. John Philip Anderson Morshead and Alethea Yonge, he graduated from University College Oxford in 1869, and qualified as a barrister at the Middle Temple in 1873. He married (21 April 1880) his cousin Helen Beatrice Anderson Morshead (1853/4-1922). He was interested in local history and has an obituary in Transactions of the Devonshire Association 55,56 (1924).

description: brother of Mary Anderson Morshead, perhaps retarded or an invalid

biography: She married (25 April 1884) Charles William Vanustegen Stewart (b.1859), solicitor, of Plymouth.

description: son of John Yonge Anderson Morshead

biography: third son of Captain Pentyre Anderson Morshead (1822/3-1869), he matriculated at St. Edmund Hall in 1875. [Alumni Oxonienses]

Brother of the Rev. John Philip Anderson Morshead, he was first cousin to WCY and to the Rev. John Yonge of Puslinch.  Described as half-pay captain Royal Artillery in 1861 census, he married (1843) Charlotte Story (1823/4-1888).
she married Captain Pentyre Anderson Morshead and had a large family.  Her birth date sometimes appears 1820/1.

Third son of Rev. John Philip Anderson Morshead and Alethea Yonge, he was a brilliant child and educated at Winchester and New College, Oxford 1867-72. He got a double first and returned to serve as assistant master at Winchester College 1872-1904. He married (1 Aug 1878) Mary, fourth sister of William Andrewes Fearon, headmaster of Winchester College 1884-91. He died of General Paralysis of the Insane after having spent some months in Holloway Sanatorium [Winchester College Register;  Wainewright, Winchester College; ODNB; LG 1871 Morshead; Hants RO MS 67M922W/82/21]

He matriculated from Exeter Coll 1827 and from 1854 was Vicar of Salcombe Regis.  His grandmother was Elizabeth Yonge, sister of the Rev. Duke Yonge, Vicar of Cornwood, so he and his brother Captain Pentyre Anderson Morshead were cousins of the Yonges of Puslinch and of CMY.  He married (1845) his second cousin Alethea Yonge (1815-1863), eldest daughter of the Rev. John Yonge of Puslinch.

description: Master of St. Cross Hospital from 1868
probable member of the Gosling Society
biography: Fourth daughter of  of Sir Thomas Dyke Acland, 11th Bt. (1809–1898), she married (1885) Frederick Henry Anson.  She was probably a Gosling as ‘Acorn’;  her diary in Devon Record Office describes a meeting with CMY. [PB 1914]
He succeeded his uncle by special remainder, 1826, and was succeeded by his son and namesake (1818-1899).

description: contributor to MP (1899) and editor of The Antiquary

biography: Daughter of the Rev. Thomas Archer Houblon (1808-1874) and Eleanor Deedes (d.1865).  A Gosling as Polypodium, she lived in December 1876 at Peasmore Rectory, Newbury.  Her father had been one of W.J. Butler's curates at Wantage;  her only brother, the Rev.  T. H. Archer Houblon (1849-1933) succeeded him as Vicar of Wantage, 1881-1907, and Maria kept house for him.  She became an Associate of the Wantage sisterhood in 1870.  Of their three sisters Eleanor (d. 1917) became an associate in 1866;  Sophia (1844-1927) became a professed sister of the community in 1878 and Reverend Mother 1912-1920; and Louisa Margaret (d. 1924) became an associate in 1871, professed sister in 1880 and Reverend Mother of the daughter house of the Holy Rood, Worthing.  They were cousins of other Goslings Elisabeth Forbes and Rachel Deedes and were also related to the Bramstons [LG 1952, Lady Anne Archer Houblon, The Houblon Family;  Wantage archives;  WWW;  Journal of Clarissa Trant]

description: Second cousin of CMY, a barrister who emigrated to New Zealand
biography: CMY’s grandfather, the Rev. Duke Yonge, Vicar of Cornwood, had a sister who married into the Archer family, he was her grandson.  He was a brother of the Rev. Samuel Harward Archer and of the Rev. Charles Harward Archer. [LG 1952 Archer of Trelaske]

CMY’s grandfather, the Rev. Duke Yonge, Vicar of Cornwood, had a sister who married into the Archer family, so they were relations. He was a brother of [[person:51]Fulbert Archer] and of the Rev. Samuel Harward Archer. [LG 1952 Archer of Trelaske]

CMY’s grandfather, the Rev. Duke Yonge, Vicar of Cornwood, had a sister who married into the Archer family, so they were relations.  He was a brother of Fulbert Archer and the Rev. Charles Harward Archer. [LG 1952 Archer of Trelaske]

description: contributor to MP (1898) and other periodicals as \'Henley I. Arden\'
biography: Henrietta Knight was editor, under this pseudonym, of Friendly Leaves, 1890-1899. She became editor of another GFS periodical, the Girls\' Quarterly, in 1900. Henley in Arden is a town in Warwickshire. [COPAC]

description: contributor to MP (1886), possibly the same as H. I. Arden, see Henrietta Knight

biography: Daughter of the Very Rev. Marsham Argles (1814-1892) and Margaret Julia Davys (1816/7-1898), she was one of the first students at Lady Margaret Hall and later worked for it both as an administrator and in its settlement work.  [LG 1952 Argles of Sibson]

Known as Julia, daughter of the Rt. Rev. George Davys (1780–1864), Bishop of Peterborough, she married (24 October 1839) the Very Rev. Marsham Argles (1814-1892). Her large family included Edith Argles, Marsham Argles, Alice Rawnsley and Agnes (\'Dolly\') Thicknesse.

description: Rector of Barnack, Northamptonshire, and Dean of Peterborough.
biography: He married (24 October 1839)  (Margaret) Julia Davys (b.1816/7-1898), whom CMY had known from childhood. [LG Argles of Sibson]
illustrator of CMY’s The Pupils of St. John the Divine.

He married, first, Sarah (Vine) Arnold (Otterbourne 1821/2-1896).  In the 1861 census she is a spinster farmer of 39 with a companion niece Marianna Vine (b.1843/4) and he is her boarder, aged 26.  He married, secondly in Chelsea in the fourth quarter of 1896, Ellen Vine. He was keeping a hotel in Colchester with his wife Ellen (b. Hargham, Norfolk 1853/4) in 1901.  However, since his second wife seems to be the  Ellen (Drane) Vine (b. Hargham, Norfolk 1853/4), widow and milliner, living with her father in London in 1881 and 1891, it looks as if CMY’s suspicions that he had married within the forbidden limits were unfounded.  Marriage with a deceased wife’s niece was illegal in England and Wales until the passing of the Marriage (Prohibited Degrees) Relationship Act (1931).
A lifelong friend of Keble and Sir John Taylor Coleridge.

Mentioned, as a missionary who came to South Africa in 1861-2 and looked after orphans, by A.E.M. Anderson Morshead, A Pioneer and Founder: Reminiscences of Some who Knew Robert Gray D D, First Bishop of Cape Town (London: Skeffington 1905), and presumably the Miss Arthur referred to by CMY (6 Dec 1866). See \'The Ladies\' Association, or, Great Causes Helped by Small Means\' MP (May 1867) 510: \'Little native girls may also be maintained in such boarding-schools as the Missions possess. Such may be found at Miss Arthur\'s, at the Cape, where the cost is £6 per annum\'. See the website of the institution today at http://www.st-georges.org.za/about.html

description: mentioned (30 Sept 1844) as a reader of Abbeychurch, unknown to CMY
contributor to MP (1867-77) and to the Monthly Paper of Sunday Teaching
biography: He married (1854) Elizabeth Fixsen (b. 1822/3). He served from 1870 as principal of Chichester Theological College, from 1864-76 he was editor of the Literary Churchman and from 1876 of the Church Quarterly Review.

title: Duke of Cadiz
biography: He married (1846) his double first cousin Queen Isabella II.

description: sister of Ann Carter Smith and contributor to MP
biography: She contributed to MP (1855-7) five papers on ‘Traditions of Norway’, with which she had probably become acquainted while the family lived there. Daughter of the Rev. Richard Carter Smith and sister of Ann Carter Smith,  she was christened St. Olave, Hart Street, London, 13 September 1827, and married (1856), on his being appointed Master of Clare College, the Rev. Dr. Edward Atkinson (1819-1915), and died childless.  He was the longest-serving ever head of a Cambridge College.  In his obituary in  The Times  (3 March 1915) 13d, she is described as a niece of a former fellow and tutor of the college (i.e. William Williamson).
He preached at Babbacombe in 1867.

description: a friend of Anne Yonge's or their governess?
son of the Rev. James Edward Austen Leigh
nephew and biographer of Jane Austen
daughter of the Rev. Vere Awdry
partner in W.H. Smith and Son, newsagents
biography: Son of Sir John Wither Awdry (1795-1878), chief justice of Bombay, brother of Frances Awdry,  the Rt. Rev. William Awdry and the Rev. Vere Awdry,he married (1876) CMY’s goddaughter Margaret Helen Moberly. Sir John Awdry’s mother Jane Bigg was the sister of Sir William Heathcote’s mother Elizabeth (Bigg) Heathcote, and he was therefore cousin to Sir William and to the Rev. William Bigg Wither.

She was a member of the Gosling Society as ‘Humble Bee’ approximately 1859-1868. Always known as Emily, she was goddaughter to CMY\'s mother FMY.  Daughter of the Rt. Rev. George Moberly, she married (4 August 1868) the Rt. Rev. William Awdry (1842-1910). While he was a schoolmaster at Winchester, they both promoted the extension lectures.

The  author of biographies of Patteson, William Heathcote and Anne Mackenzie, she is  not to be confused with her sister-in-law, (Frances) Emily (Moberly) Awdry. The daughter of Sir John Wither Awdry (1795-1878), chief justice of Bombay, sister of the Rt. Rev. William Awdry, Charles Awdry and the Rev. Vere Awdry, she lived with her mother at Notton. Sir John Awdry’s mother Jane Bigg was the sister of Sir William Heathcote’s mother Elizabeth (Bigg) Heathcote, and he was therefore cousin to Sir William and to the Rev. William Bigg Wither. Two of Frances Awdry\'s brothers married daughters of the Rt. Rev. Dr George Moberly.  

Photographs of the family appear at http://www.family-forest.co.uk/familytree/albums/awdry/awdry-photo.shtml
Youngest daughter of the Rt Rev George Moberly, she married (20 April 1876) Charles Awdry (1847-1912), whose brother William had earlier married her sister Emily.

He succeeded John Frewen Moor as Vicar of Ampfield. He married first (3 August 1887), Emily Man, secondly (27 October 1891), Mary Louisa Man, and thirdly (14 July 1909) Lucy Louisa Bury.  He was father by his third marriage of the Rev. Wilbert Vere Awdry (1911-1997), the author of Thomas the Tank Engine (1946). Son of Sir John Wither Awdry (1795-1878), chief justice of Bombay, he was brother of Frances Awdry, the Rt. Rev. William Awdry and Charles Awdry. Sir John Awdry’s mother Jane Bigg was the sister of Sir William Heathcote’s mother Elizabeth (Bigg) Heathcote, and he was therefore cousin to Sir William and to the Rev. William Bigg Wither.

description: Vicar of Amport, later Bishop of Osaka
biography: Successively Vicar of Amport, suffragan bishop of Southampton (1895),  Bishop of Osaka (1896-8) and South Tokyo (1898-1908), he married (4 August 1868) (Frances) Emily Moberly. Son of Sir John Wither Awdry (1795-1878), chief justice of Bombay, he was brother of Frances Awdry,  Charles Awdry and the Rev. Vere Awdry. His brother Charles Awdry married Margaret Helen Moberly. Sir John Awdry’s mother Jane Bigg was the sister of Sir William Heathcote’s mother Elizabeth (Bigg) Heathcote, and he was therefore cousin to Sir William and to the Rev. William Bigg Wither.  [WWW]

description: a pupil of CMY at Otterbourne school
biography: She married a soldier and just died three weeks after the birth of her baby.  She was probably daughter of James Backhurst (b. 1800/1), carpenter, of Otterbourne.

description: companion of Maria Cristall (Florence Wilford\'s aunt) at St. Cross

biography: CMY refused a garden party invitation from, n. d.

description: Archdeacon of George, then of the Cape, later Bishop of Capetown
biography: CMY sent her books to him.

description: daughter of General Sir Richard Wilbraham
biography: She married (4 April 1872) George Barrington Baker (1845–1912), who succeeded his father as 5th Bt. in 1912.
She married the Rev. Sir Talbot Baker, 3rd Bt. (1820-1900) and is mentioned as an author, 1888.

This person teaching Joanna Yonge is probably to be identified as Agnes Baker (b.1863/4), daughter of the Rev. James Baker of Clifton Lodge, Winchester, who is described, like her sister Emily (b. 1858/9) in the 1891 census as a Teacher of Music.
The Rev. James Baker of Clifton Lodge, Winchester, seems the most plausible Mr Baker.

Described as a new Gosling as ‘Sparrowhawk’ in September 1867, she was living at Upper East Hayes, Bath, and was daughter of Major Thomas Richard Baker (1802-1884) J.P., 7th Fusiliers Rtd. and Mary Frances Anderson Morshead (d. 1843).  She was first cousin to fellow Goslings [[person:28]Mary] and Beatrice Anderson Morshead, and was related to CMY through her great-grandmother. [LG 1906 Baker of Bayfordbury, 1871 census]
He is recorded in the 1881 and 1891 censuses as a maltster living at Compton with his wife Josephine (b. Solihull 1826/7), in the former year ‘employing 2 men & 2 boys’.

description: listed as a contributor to the Hursley Magazine in 1848

biography: He was the author of the first standard work on English surnames and contributor to the Bluebell series [BL cat; Alumni Oxonienses]

Coleridge states, [[otherbook:40]Life], 154 that CMY\'s grandmother died in 1848. However, it seems more probable that she died in 1843, when the death was registered in Winchester of a person of that name. She was daughter of the Rev. Thomas Kingsman (1717-1779), Vicar of Botley, and married (1792), as his second wife, the Rev. Thomas Bargus. \'I think she was 89\' when she died, wrote CMY. The IGI records the christening of a Mary Kingsman at Botley in 1751, which would make her about 92 in 1843, and 44 at the time of FMY\'s birth in 1795. Her father\'s death is recorded in the Town and Country Magazine (1780), 55.
Her age is given differently in the 1851 and 1841 censuses.

description: Vicar of Barkway, maternal grandfather of CMY
biography: He married first (1787), a widow with two children, Cordelia (Garstin) Colborne (d.15 March 1791) and secondly (1792) Mary Kingsman. [LG 1870 Garstin of Leragh Castle]
The context of these references suggests a Puslinch neighbour.

Third of the five daughters of the Rev. Edward Barlee, Rector of Worlingworth, Suffolk, she was Lady superintendent of the Institution for the Employment of Needlewomen, Hinde St, founded 1860, as well as a contributor to the Athenaeum, the Englishwoman's Journal and MP (1866), referred to 3 April 1863. [1851, 1861 census]

description: mother of the Rev. Henry Bowles
biography: Daughter of Robert Barlow of Holybourne, she was wife of the Rev. Henry Albany Bowles, sr..

description: composer and poet under the name 'Claribel', contributor to MP (1869)
perhaps a neighbour of the Puslinch Yonges.
biography: He may possibly also be the Barnes referred to by FMY in 1854 as acting on behalf of WCY in Devon.

description: sister-in-law of the Very Rev. William John Butler
biography: Second cousin of the Very Rev. William Butler, who was married to her younger sister Emma Barnett, she supported his good works at Wantage.  She lived with her father George Henry Barnett (d. 1871) and younger sister Louisa at Glympton and in Wilton Crescent. [H. Barnett, Glympton;  LG 1952 Barnett formerly of Glympton]

description: daughter of the Rt. Rev. George Moberly
biography: She married (10 Sept 1863) the Rev. Henry Barter (1835/6-1901), from 1868 Vicar of Shipton-under-Wychwood. Referred to as Kitty Barter, she is not to be confused with Kate Barter, her sister-in-law, or with her husband’s cousin Katharine Mary (Barter) Wordsworth (d.1897). [Dulce Domum]

He married (10 Sept 1863) Elspeth Catherine Moberly, known as Kitty Barter; he also had a sister Kate Barter who ran a school in Shipton. Son of the Rev. Charles Barter, Vicar of Sarsden, he was educated at Eton and Merton College Oxford, and became Vicar of Shipton-under-Wychwood in 1868. [Eton Register; Alumni Oxonienses]

The daughter of the Rev. Charles Barter, Rector of Sarsden, and niece of the Rev. Robert Speckott Barter, she seems to have lived near her brother the Rev. Henry Barter, Vicar of Shipton-under-Wychwood, and run (in 1871) a small school, whose pupils included a South African ward named Salome Melango. CMY calls her ‘Kate Barter’ and refers to her ‘young Zulus’. She is not to be confused with her sister-in-law Elspeth Catherine ‘Kitty’ (Moberly) Barter, or with her first cousin Katherine Mary (Barter) Wordsworth. She was the author of an anonymous travel book Alone among the Zulus: The narrative of a journey through the Zulu country, South Africa. By a plain woman (London: SPCK 1866) and has an entry in S. O. Spencer, British settlers in Natal, 1824-1857: A Biographical Register (2001). She was born at Broadstone, Oxfordshire.

description: mother of the Rev. Robert Speckott Barter
biography: Widow of the Rev. Charles Barter, Vicar of Cornworthy. Her death reported in the Morning Post (26 January 1850).
A much-loved figure. [Wainewright, Winchester College]
Eldest son of Edmund Rodney Pollexfen Bastard (1784-1838) of Kitley, very near Puslinch, he converted to Rome and married (1853) Florence Mary Scrope (d. 1871) [LG 1952)
He succeeded his brother Edmund Bastard in the Kitley estates.

Daughter of Chaplin Aaron Harris of Evergreen, Baltimore USA she married (4 Dec 1873), as his second wife, Charles Edward Barrett Lennard (1835-July 1874). Evidently a novelist who lived in Germany, and a moaner. Fiction exists published by Mrs Charles Edward Barrett Lennard. The identification of CMY’s correspondent with this person seems likely but cannot be certain.[PB 1914; 1881, 1901 London census]

Daughter of the Rev. Henry Stebbing, her marriage (24 July 1860) to the Rev. Robert Braithwaite Batty, elder son of the late Lieut-Col Robert Batty, Grenadier Guards, was announced in The Times (26 July 1860). She appears to have been sister-in-law to Johanna Batty. According to her obituary The Times (2 May 1933) her husband went as a missionary to India and died almost immediately. Some autobiographical and other MSS of hers are in the Bodleian Library, Oxford.

description: contributor to MP as Ivanovna (1862-91), social worker and writer
biography: She lived with her mother (born in South Africa, daughter of Sir John Barrow Bt., 1764-1848, the geographer) and sister at 140 Hampstead Road in London.  She collaborated with CMY on a guide to charities of England but it is not clear whether it was published [1851, 1881 census].

Daughter of William Rutter Bayley (1813/4-1879), J.P. of Cotford House, Sidbury, Sidmouth, she was  a Gosling as ‘Hoopoe’ [Devon 1851 census;  PO Devon 1873, Alumni Oxonienses; his will, he left 70,000]

description: headmistress of Cheltenham Ladies College, contributor to MP (1882)

title: 6th Earl Beauchamp
biography: He succeeded his brother in 1866 and married, first (18 Feb 1868), Lady Mary Catherine Stanhope (d. 30 June 1876), and, secondly (24 Sept 1878), Lady Emily A C Pierrepoint (d. 1935).

description: stepmother of Gertrude Walter and Frances (Walter) Yonge
biography: She married first (1853) Lieut-Colonel Edward Walter (1804-10 Dec 1862),  and secondly (1867), the Rev. James Beck (b.1819/20), Rector of Parham and then of Bildeston.

description: contributor to MP (1869), Rector of St. Mary Rotherhithe
husband of Gertrude Walter’s stepmother, Rector of Parham, Sussex, and then of Bildeston, Suffolk
biography: He became in 1871 Rector of Parham transferring by 1881 to of Bildeston, Suffolk, and serving as Rural Dean of Suffolk.  He married (1867)  Gertrude Walter’s stepmother Caroline Jeannette (Bignell) Walter.

description: owner of gloves associated with Charles I
biography: Her address is given as Malmain, French hay, Bristol, where she is found in the 1891 census as the French-born wife of William Belfield, J.P..

description: friend of Ruskin and headmistress of Winnington Hall School
biography: See The Winnington Letters: John Ruskin\'s Correspondence with Margaret Alexis Bell (1969).

description: writer on art and travel as N. DAnvers, contributor to MP (1883)
contributor to MP (1866), author of fiction and non-fiction 1848-1885
biography: The daughter of the Rev. Henry Bellairs, Rector of Bedworth, Warwickshire, she lived in Bournemouth for the latter part of her life.
He married (1821) Emily Moberly, daughter of Edward Moberly of St Petersburg and sister of Rt. Rev. George Moberly [LG 1906]

description:

The Miss Bennett, known to Louisa Catherine Palmer, who had eye trouble in 1864, might be the same person, or not.
writer, son of Archbishop Benson, contributor to MP (1896)

biography: Jemima (Wedderburn) Blackburn (1823-1909), a Scottish naturalist and painter, met CMY through [[person:1252]Frederic Rogers] (1811-1889), later Lord Blachford, a Devon Tractarian who was married to her cousin Georgina Colvile (d.1900). Blackburn’s memories of CMY are printed in Robert Fairley, [[otherbook:63]Jemima: Paintings and Memoirs of a Victorian Lady] (Edinburgh : Canongate, 1988), 128: ‘Charlotte Yonge was a friend of the Rogers and was asked to stay while I was visiting them. It was a very small house and we were lodged in two little garrets next one another, and used to brush out our hair together before going to bed, and so soon became friends. She was very good looking with dark hair and fine eyes, spoke pleasantly and was a little above middle height. We talked of many things. I found her not at all formidable, as one feared she might be, being so well informed; one might almost say learned. . . . I kept up the friendship as long as she lived, and got a good many letters from her while I was illustrating her books.’ She married Hugh Blackburn, Professor of Mathematics at Edinburgh University. Jemima Blackburn discovered the habits of the cuckoo.

description: perpetual curate of Charlton-next-Woolwich, father of Ann Carter Smith
biography: He was christened Morwenstow, Cornwall, 29 August 1802, son of William and Ann Smith; and married, at Campton, near Bedford, on 24 November 1825, Mary Williamson, daughter of the Rev. Edmund (Boase has Edmond) Williamson (c.1760-1839), Rector of Campton with Shefford, Beds., and his wife Phoebe Riland.  Smith was admitted, late in life, a fellow commoner at Caius College, Cambridge in 1844, proceeded BA and MA in 1849 and 1860, was ordained deacon in 1848 and priest in 1849.  He served as curate of Sutton Coldfield, Warwickshire 1848-50, Pershore 1851-3, Stepney 1854-7, and Charlton-next-Woolwich from 1862, being appointed to the perpetual curacy of St. Pauls Charlton.  He died aged 62 on 1 October 1864. It looks as if Richard Carter Smith was emulating one of his brothers-in-law in retraining for the church in the crisis years of the early 1840s, and that after he was ordained he acted as curate to another brother-in-law for five years. He has  BL or Copac entries but the Harvard library catalogue lists Richard Carter Smith, Reise i Norge 1838 overs av Johnny Johnsen (Oslo, Univertitesforl c.1976). This corroborates the evidence that the Carter Smith family had spent time in Norway. [IGI; Alumni Cantabrigienses, there is a brief death notice in the Gentleman's Magazine.]

Thomas Clarke, Rector of Woodeaton, Oxford, and Louisa Lane, author of topographical and historical works on the Channel Islands, she married (1879) Bartholomew (or Bartle) Teeling (1848-1921), Captain in the Rifle Brigade, Secretary 1872 of the Catholic Union of Ireland, Private Chamberlain to the Pope.  She published journalism, a story, a play, music, sometimes as 'Norman Stuart' or 'Isola.  [WWW both husband and wife, Priaulx Library, wills index.]

Author of Lives of the Princesses of Wales. She was born in Whitchurch, Shropshire, daughter of a solicitor there, and married (1883) the Rev. Henry Brumell Finch (b.1849).
He is mentioned in connection with the Bullock project. Several possible candidates.

She is described as contributing sketches of good works among negroes to Mission Life 1867. She and her mother are mentioned as friends in Elizabeth Sewell\'s autobiography, which was probably how the correspondence with CMY arose. She was the daughter of Sarah Paine Perkins and Henry Russell Cleveland (1808-1843) and was brought up in the New England political and literary establishment. She was the niece of the art collector Edward Newton Perkins (1820-1899) and was travelling with him and her mother in Italy in 1859 when they were attacked by local revolutionaries, causing a diplomatic incident. Eugene Hollahan \'Intertextual Bondings Between \\"The Wreck of the Hesperus\\" and \\"The Wreck of the Deutschland\\"\' Texas Studies in Literature and Language 33 (1991) discusses her correspondence with Longfellow which she communicated to CMY who published it in MP. There is a large collection of the Cleveland and Perkins papers in the New York Public Library.

Possibly James Francis Cobb, novelist.
He succeeded the Rt. Rev. John Coleridge Patteson as head of the mission to Melanesia; he was author of a Mota Dictionary and ethnographical works on Melanesia.

title: 1st Lord Seaton
biography: He married (21 June 1814) Elizabeth Yonge (7 March 1790-28 Nov 1872).  He was created a peer in 1839, and  made Field Marshal in 1860.  WCY was in his regiment, was first cousin to his wife, and married his stepsister.

title: Lady Seaton
biography: Sister of the Rev. John Yonge of Puslinch, she married  (21 June 1814) Sir John Colborne, 1st Lord Seaton (1778-1863).

title: 2nd Lord Seaton
biography: He married (12 Feb 1851) the Hon. Charlotte de Burgh.  CMY and her mother were present at his wedding, which was reported in The Times (14 February 1851): \'On the 12th inst., by special licence, at St. Peter\'s Church, Pimlico, by the Rev. John Yonge, rector of Newton Ferrers, assisted by the Rev. Dr. Harris, incumbent of Tor Mohun, Major the Hon. James Colborne, eldest son of Lieutenant-General Lord Seaton, to the Hon. Charlotte de Burgh, youngest daughter of Lieutenant-General Lord Downes.\' [PB 1914; tomb Newton Ferrars church]

title: Lady Seaton
biography: Daughter of the last Lord Downes, she died a week after her husband inherited his father’s title.  Her sister Anne de Burgh (d. 1872) married (1838) the 3rd Earl of Clonmell.

description: member of the Gosling Society, cousin of CMY
biography: The daughter of James, 2nd Lord Seaton and the Hon. Charlotte de Burgh (d. 1863) she was granddaughter of FMY's stepbrother Field-Marshal Lord Seaton.  She was a Gosling as ‘Bluebell’ from 1870. [PB 1914, wills index]

title: 3rd Lord Seaton
biography: Grandson of the 1st Lord Seaton, he succeeded his father as 3rd Lord Seaton 1888.  He assumed  the additional surnames Fuller-Elliott-Drake after marrying the heiress of that family.
The daughter of the 1st Lord Seaton [tombstone Holy Cross, Newton Ferrars; PB 1914]
Eldest daughter of the 1st Lord Seaton. [PB 1914;  tombstone Holy Cross, Newton Ferrars; 1871 census]

He married (1873) Rhoda Ellen Blogg (1843-1913) and had one daughter, (b.1876).  Rhoda (Blogg) Colborne is listed in the 1861 census as a governess and in the 1891 census as inspectress for the Education Department.

biography: He is probably the Frank Colborne having trouble with his ears (1870) rather than his uncle General the Hon. Sir Francis Colborne (1817-1895).
Second son of the 1st Lord Seaton, he was probably not the Frank Colborne having trouble with his ears in 1870.

title: 4th Lord Seaton
biography: Third third son of the 2nd Lord Seaton, he succeeded his eldest brother as 4th Lord Seaton in 1933.

description: correspondent, evidently a friend of the Colborne family.
biography: If the book she sent CMY in 1874 was Nina Cole, Meditations on the Song of Songs (London: Hayes 1874), an anonymous volume identified by Halkett and Laing, that may have been her name. A person of this name was a committee member of the Church and Stage Guild (founded 1879). Its objects, according to an advertisement in The Era (13 July 1879) were \'to promote religious and social sympathy between the members of the Church and of the Stage\'. However, another possible candidate is Anna Cole (1832/3-1909), daughter of the Rev. John Francis Cole, Vicar of Kirdford, near Petworth, Sussex, who was a subscriber to MP and appears in its correspondence column (December 1877) 592.

description: member of the Gosling Society, cousin of CMY
biography: Much the youngest daughter of Francis Coleridge (1794-1854); her mother sank into depression after her birth and she was brought up by her elder sister Harriet Duke (Coleridge) Lowe (b.1829/30), wife of the Rev. Edward Clarke Lowe (1823-1912) one of the moving spirits in the Woodard Schools movement for the education of the middle classes.  She lived with them at The College, Hurstpierpoint, and was a Gosling as ‘Gurgoyle’ 1863-after 1869.  She became Lady Warden of St. Anne's Abbot's Bromley, a Woodard girls' school, c. 1874 and spent the rest of her life there. Her brother Arthur Duke Coleridge was father of Mary E. Coleridge, the poet.  She was CMY's goddaughter.  It looks from the Barnacle as if she spent some time living with Mildred and/or Mary Coleridge.  [ODNB; Rice, Story of St. Mary's Abbot's Bromley; Coleridge, Story of a Devonshire House]

Third son of Francis Coleridge, solicitor, of Ottery (brother to Sir John Taylor Coleridge) he was the elder brother of Alice Mary Coleridge, and a cousin of Coleridge Patteson and Mary Coleridge. His mother Frances Duke (Taylor) Coleridge was a first cousin of CMY’s grandfather the Rev. Duke Yonge, so they were third cousins. [Obituaries Times 30, 31 October 1913]

Daughter of the Rev. Derwent Coleridge (1800-1883), headmaster (1826-41) of Helston Grammar School, Principal (1841-64) of St Mark\'s College, Chelsea, and Rector (1864-80) of Hanwell, Middlesex, and his wife Mary Simpson Pridham;  she was granddaughter of S. T. Coleridge.  The longest-serving member of the Gosling Society, she was called Chelsea Delf to 1863 and Chelsea China thereafter;  she acted as secretary and many members seem to have been recruited by her;  she was first cousin to Cobweb and Hedgerose; Ladybird, Gurgoyle, Pena and Cricket were more distant relations.  The move to Hanwell took place in August 1864. In 1873 she was evidently helping her brother Ernest run a school in his house at Chiddingfold. Contributor to (including Debatable Ground) and later editor of MP. From 1890 she was editor of Friendly Leaves (Jan 1876 to June 1917) a magazine, originally edited by Anne Mercier, produced by the Girls\' Friendly Society (founded 1875). Will proved £4615 [Hainton, Unknown Coleridge;  DNB; will]

description: son of the poet, uncle of Christabel Coleridge, contributor to MP (1892)

biography: Daughter of Henry Nelson Coleridge and Sara Coleridge, she moved in with the Derwent Coleridges in July 1857 aged 25. She was an artist, and may have contributed illustrations to the Barnacle. Unlike Christabel she was related to CMY, through her father, who was Sir John Taylor Coleridge\'s brother. [Hainton, Unknown Coleridge, Roels MSS genealogy]

description: master at Eton, from 1867 Vicar of Mapledurham
biography: His first wife Mary Keate (d. 1859) was the daughter of Dr Keate, headmaster of Eton;  he married secondly (1862), Mary Caroline Bevan (1822/3-1907).  He was tutor to his nephew J. C. Patteson;  recipient of sums from CMY from 1853, perhaps on Patteson\'s behalf; and a keen supporter of missionary work.

He married first (1831) Elizabeth Tucker, and, secondly (1841), Ellen Sophia Patteson. He was the son of the Rev. Edward Coleridge (1760/1-1843), Vicar of Buckerell, brother of the poet. He was therefore not related to CMY. [Alumni Oxonienses]

description: second wife of the Rev. Edwin Coleridge
biography: According to the marriage announcement Hampshire Telegraph 13 July 1841, she was the daughter of H. Patteson Esq. of Woburn Place. She may have been related to Sir John Patteson (who married her husband’s first cousin Frances Duke Coleridge in 1824) but she wasn’t his sister.

biography: [will]

biography: [Roels MS]

biography: He married first (11 Aug 1846), Jane Fortescue Seymour (1824/5-1878); and, secondly (1885) Amy Augusta Jackson Lawford (1853-1933), who had previously passed for some years as the wife of her cousin John Davies, but whose Gretna Green marriage had been declared void in 1878.  He was knighted in December 1868 on becoming solicitor general; he was created (1874) Lord Coleridge on being made chief justice of the common pleas; he became Lord Chief Justice in 1880.  [ODNB]

description: second wife of the 1st Lord Coleridge

[Lawford v Davies (1878) 4 PD 61, 47 LJP 38 P, D and Admlty]  This fact may sufficiently account for the disapproving tone of CMY\'s references to her.
She married (1903) George Herbert Gair. [Roels MS]

description: daughter of Sir [[person:344]John Taylor Coleridge], cousin and lifelong friend of CMY, member of the Gosling Society
biography: The intimacy between CMY and Mary Coleridge is not well documented because the letters to her were, Christabel Coleridge states, burnt in an accident, but she is very frequently referred to in letters to others. Her 1845 engagement to Roundell Palmer, later 1st Earl of Selborne, was broken off, and she never married. She was devoted to her niece Mildred, daughter of Lord Coleridge, and encouraged CMY to found the Gosling Society partly in order to find an outlet for Mildred\'s intellectual interests. Her Gosling name was The Old Secretary, but when Mildred lost interest in the society, she did likewise. She was devastated by the furore over Mildred\'s 1885 marriage to Charles Warren Adams, who had sued Bernard Coleridge for libel. In the same year her brother Lord Coleridge had married Amy Lawford, who had previously lived as the wife of her first cousin, but had then had their Gretna Green marriage declared invalid. It appears that Mary Coleridge, like CMY, consequently disapproved of the second Lady Coleridge, and deplored her influence on her husband. [PB: Coleridge, Story of a Devonshire House] A portrait of her and her sister Alethea as girls sold in 2006 is illustrated at www.artnet.com/Artists/LotDetailPage.aspx?lot_id=5830456F7F89012700A33CFAA5D
[Roels MSS]

After Martha\'s death he married a younger woman named Emma, who also acted as postmistress of Otterbourne, and had at least one daughter, Frances (b. 1876), who qualified as a teacher and was the mistress of Otterbourne School.

Yonge: An Interview\' Sunday Magazine (June 1901) 437-439: \'There was a keen satisfaction in the tone in which she said, \\"The little maid who let you in is a link with old times. Her grandfather was in the service of our family for sixty years.\\"\' This would be [[person:357]George Collins].

She was the wife of George Collins (b. 1818/9), of the Post Office, Otterbourne, groom and gardener, and mother of George (b. 1839/40),  Charles (b.1840/1), Olive (b.1841/2), Elizabeth (Bessie) who was one of Mary Anne Dyson\'s pupils, and Anne (b. 1846/7). [1861 census]   It is not unlikely that she was also the person,  referred to only as Martha, who worked in Misselbrook\'s shop.

Daughter of George and Martha Collins of Otterbourne, she was housemaid to the Rev. George Merriman, headmaster of Royal Grammar School, Guildford, in 1862.  She was probably working for the Moberlys in the Isle of Wight in 1869 when CMY heard via Mr Wither her report that George Moberly had been made Bishop of Salisbury.
An inhabitant of Otterbourne in 1838;  possibly the Elizabeth Comely who died Winchester Jan-Mar 1850. [Register of deaths]

Described as of Binsted Hill, Alton, he was trustee of marriage settlement of Julian Bargus Yonge and Emma Frances Walter. A bachelor gentleman farmer,  he was probably brother of Mary Emma (Coulthard) Walter and uncle to Frances Yonge. [WDRO MS]

He was the father of father of Mary Emma, James Batten and Frances Charlotte Hilare Coulthard. Deirdre Le Faye, Jane Austen’s Letters, 511, calls him James Battin Coulthard (1782-1856). The Mrs Coulthard whom Jane Austen called (11 April 1805), 99, ‘a good-hearted, friendly woman’, was, Le Faye thinks, his stepmother Frances Barlow (1764-1829), who married his father Thomas Coulthard (1756-1811) in 1784. Perhaps there was some connection with Hilare Barlow (d.1757), second wife of the first Earl Nelson, who subsequently (1837) married Austen’s nephew George Thomas Knight . [1841 census]
'old Mrs Coulthard' lived with her daughter Frances Charlotte Hilare Coulthard in Hastings in the 1861 census.
He lived in Plymstock, and was trustee of the marriage settlement of Julian Bargus Yonge and his niece Emma Frances Walter [WDRO MS]
He was evidently a partner of Charles Mozley and Walter Smith in 1874, ‘Mozley, Cowie and Smith’ appears briefly in 1874 as the imprint of the firm.

She is mentioned in  December 1849 and June 1854 as the Moberly's governess, and appears thus in the 1851 census.  She is listed as a visitor rather than governess in 1861 census, but may have been either. Later [1871 census] she seems to have become a sister of mercy in St. Elizabeth's House, Covent Garden.

A Miss H. L. Cox was the recipient of payments from CMY from 1857. Harriet Lucy Cox, who later married the Rev. Arthur Baker, was presented with a copy of The Daisy Chain by CMY (10 June 1858), inscribed \'H.L. Cox, from her sincere friend C M Yonge\'. Mrs Baker transcribed books into Braille, and it is possible that the payments relate to that, but it seems more likely that she was a contributor. [Information from Ms Delia Twamley, who owns the book.] The census returns show a Harriet E. L. Cox (b. Waddesdon Bucks. 1825/6), daughter of the Rev. Frederick Cox, Vicar of Upper Winchendon, who married the Rev. Arthur Baker (1817-1868), and is presumed to be this person. Since [[otherbook:8]\'Sunlight in the Clouds\'] was signed H.L.C. when it appeared in MP it is possible that she was the author of that work and therefore also of \'[[otherbook:5]An Object in Life\'].
He succeeded The Rev. Merton Smith as Vicar of St. Mary’s Plympton.

Coxe became  Bodley's Librarian in 1860.  He was father of Susan Esther (Coxe) Wordsworth, the first wife of the Rt. Rev. John Wordsworth.  CMY had probably met him through her friendship with the Rev. Edwards Sewell and his sister Janetta. [ODNB]

A partner in Macmillan, he married (29 April 1865) the novelist Dinah Maria Mulock (1826-1887).

CMY’s correspondent has evidently answered a Puzzled Mother in MP in 1896. Isolda Caroline Vereker (1852/3-1927), daughter of the 4th Viscount Gort and wife of Sir Charles Craufurd 4th Bt. (1847-1939), R.N..

She was the daughter of George Abraham Crawley (1795-1862), solicitor, and granddaughter of the Rev. Charles Crawley (1756-1849), Rector of Stowe Nine Churches and brother of CMY\'s grandmother Catharina (Crawley) Yonge. After her return from South Africa Edith Crawley seems to have lived with her brother, also the Rev. Charles Crawley. [Morshead, Robert Gray]

Richard Cresswell, was a clergyman without cure of souls in the 1881 census; they lived at Teignmouth.

He entered the 37th Hampshire Regiment in 1878; he became captain in 1884; went to Staff College 1890-1891; and retired from the army in 1892. He married, first (1881) Mary Grace Webb Bowen, and had at least one son born in 1882. He married, secondly (1894), CMY’s niece Joanna Angela Yonge. He served as Vice-Consul at Dar-al-Baida, Morocco, 1894-1899; and Algeciras, 1899-1902; and was Consul at Dakar and for the Republic of Liberia, 1902-1905. Cromie and Francis Cromie (1882-1918]]

He had children by his first marriage, including one who was killed in the Russian Revolution. [WWW the son; wills index, she left £637]

He served as curate of Yealmton 1866-71, and was Vicar of Sparkwell 1884.  He married (1867) Annie Hall Thomas (1836-1918), the novelist. [tablet in All Saints, Sparkwell]

biography: The wife of the Rev. George Herbert Curteis (1823/4-1894), head of Lichfield Theological College in 1861, Rector of Waldron, Sussex in 1881, chaplain of Royal Savoy Chapel in 1891, she wrote a life of Bishop Selwyn , and children\'s verse. Another possible candidate for this Mrs Curteis is Frances Curteis (1816/7-1887), mother of Bessie Charlotte Curteis, a known contributor.

This person was author, as Bessie C. Curteis, of In the Marsh (SPCK 1876). East Sussex Record Office MS AMS6128/3/27 is a letter (June 1875) from Bessie Charlotte Curteis to her father Edward Barrett Curteis of Leasam House, Rye, Sussex, stating that she has been offered £50 for the manuscript of her article in the Monthly Packet. She was no doubt the \'B.C.C.\' who wrote \'On Dialect\' MP (February 1874) 171-184. It therefore seems reasonable to assume that she is the \'Miss Curteis\' of Leasams to whom CMY was writing about \'your eagle and goose story\', in a letter probably dating from 1872. Her mother Frances Curteis (1816/7-1887) might have been the Mrs Curteis to whom CMY addressed a letter of 1878, but Elizabeth A. Curteis seems more plausible

Ordained (1863) by the Bishop of Winchester, he served as curate of Alverstoke, Hants 1862-67, and Christ Church, Albany Street, London 1867-70. He served as secretary of the National Society for the Education of the Poor in Accordance with the Principles of the Established Church from 1871 till 1891 when he resigned to become a canon of Canterbury. [MS Lambeth Palace 4503 ff.63-5, letter from E.W. Benson; Crockfords; brief obituary Leeds Mercury (12 January 1895); canonry Daily News 26 May 1891.]
He succeeded to Ochtertyre; he married.

description: nephew of Anne Mackenzie, an invalid

title: Lord Manour
description: Scots judge, brother-in-law of Anne Mackenzie
biography: A Scots judge, he was styled Lord Manour from 1868; he married Elizabeth Mackenzie (d.1858) and had four daughters and five sons; he was brother-in-law of Anne Mackenzie and father of Mary Dundas.
[ODNB] James, Colin and George Dundas also had two younger brothers, William John Dundas (1849-1921) and David Dundas (1854-1922).

She contributed articles on the Cambridge Local Examination, and perhaps also the other articles signed \'L. D.\' (1875-89). From the obituary \'L. Dundas\' contributed to MP (1887) (2) 151, of her youngest sister Adela Dundas (1840-1887) it is clear that she cannot be Katharine Louisa Dundas (b. 1849), youngest sister of Mary Frances Dundas. It is also clear from this source that her father died in 1883. She was probably the Louisa Dundas christened in February 1834, daughter of William Pitt Dundas (d.1883), Registrar General of Scotland, and his cousin and wife Mary Strange, whose daughter Adela was christened 1840 (there were several other children too). He was a member of the family of Dundas of Arniston.

description: member of the Gosling Society, niece of Anne Mackenzie
biography: Daughter of George Dundas (1802-1869), from 1868 styled Lord Manour, Senator of the College of Justice in Scotland, and his wife Elizabeth Mackenzie (d. 1858), elder sister of Anne Mackenzie.  A Gosling as ‘Ladyfern\' between 1863-before 1869, she was responsible for binding the Barnacle, and CMY thought her careless about it.  [LG 2001; LG 1906 Mackenzie;  Grant, Faculty of Advocates ]
He was Bishop of Quebec 1892-1914

She offered Good Friday, another story about Ottavia, to MP in 1889; she may have lived abroad. Both 'Ottavia' MP 1887(2) 87 and 'A Good Friday Procession at Grassina' MP (1890) (1) 371 appeared under the name 'E.Vere'.

description: an inhabitant of Otterbourne (24 Sept 1846), either a schoolmistress or a parent
biography: Perhaps Maria Durndell (b. 1824/5) wife of James Durndell, of Otterbourne.
Known as 'the Simorg', he lived with his wife (who was his cousin) and his much younger half-sister Mary Anne Dyson at Dogmersfield Rectory from 1836.

description: wife and cousin of the Rev. Charles Dyson
biography: They married at Wexham 21 April 1819 [IGI; his ODNB entry]

The Rev. Francis Dyson (b.London 1818/19), Vicar of St. Sampson, Cricklade, had daughters Penelope Francis (b.1848/9) and Charlotte Cara (b.1852/3) and son Francis (b. 1849/50) [1861, 1871, 1881 census].  He was the son of the Rev. Canon Francis Dyson (1784/5-1858), Rector of North and South Tedworth, who was brother to the Rev. Charles Dyson, Rector of Dogmersfield.  In the 1851 census Canon Dyson was living in Great Malvern.

Life-long friend of CMY, she lived with her much older half-brother, the Rev. Charles Dyson, Rector of Dogmersfield, until his death in 1860, and latterly at Church Crookham. Her will was proved by her nephew the Rev Francis Dyson, estate under £10,000. She was an invalid ‘confined her to a sofa and latterly even to her bed’ ; author of Conversations with Cousin Rachel, Little Alice and her Sister, The White Kitten, Out in the Dark, Ivo and Verena, [wills index, obit MP (1878, 2, 521-5]
He bought Silkstead Priors in Compton parish and was living there in the 1901 census.

description: Matron of Andover Industrial School for Girls

biography: She was author of devotional verse, a friend of Elizabeth Barrett Browning, a spiritualist medium and probably also the Mrs Eckley contributing to MP in 1873.

title: 3rd Lord Auckland
description: Bishop of Sodor and Man, 1847-54, and of Bath and Wells, 1854-69

biography: She married (1889) Thomas Bainbridge Eden (b.1856/7), schoolmaster; she contributed to MP (1874).
Her address is the Cottage, Alvesford [Alresford?], she appears to have been connected with the GFS.
Sister of Margaret (Scott) Gatty. She became a Roman Catholic. [Maxwell, Mrs Gatty and Mrs Ewing, 54]

description: eldest son of the Rev. W. F. Elgie
biography: He left Lancing 1889, and resigned his commission in 1904. He was a colonial administrator for twenty years.  [Lancing Register;  tablet in Otterbourne Church]

description: son of the Rev. W. F. Elgie
daughter of the Rev. W. F. Elgie
wife of the Rev. W. F. Elgie
biography: She married first (1858) Captain William George Everard Webber and had at least three children, then (1869) the Rev. Walter Francis Elgie (1837-1881), and had six more.  She seems to have changed the spelling of the name to Elgee.

description: second son of the Rev. W.F. Elgie
biography: He graduated BA from Oriel Coll Oxford 1900. [Lancing Register]

description: son of the Rev. W.F. Elgie
biography: Captain South Wales Borderers, killed in action at Gallipoli [tablet in Otterbourne Church]

He married (1869) Catharine, daughter of Colonel F. Hammond and widow of Captain Webber.  He was a scholar of Lancing 1853, MA St. Edmund Hall 1859, curate of Otterbourne 1870-6, vicar of Otterbourne 1876-81 [Lancing Register]

description: daughter of the Rev. [[person:478]W. F. Elgie], Vicar of Otterbourne, and goddaughter of CMY
biography: She married Harry Burton in 1906. [marriage index; notice about probate The Times, 16 October 1939]

She was recipient of sums from CMY from 1856, headmistress of a large [for then] girls\' school, St. Michael\'s College, Bognor. This was a school associated with the Woodard schools, and closed, as St. Michael\'s, Petworth, in 1994.  She was eldest daughter of  William, 2nd Earl of St. Germans (1767-1845). Her stepmother Susan Mordaunt was the aunt of Mary Anne Dyson\'s friend Mary (Mordaunt), Lady Acland. [PB; 1861 census]  Her successor as headmistress of St. Michael\'s was Frances Wheeler.

description: Vicar of Bitton and author of The Plant-Lore and Garden Craft of Shakespeare (1878)
biography: He was probably ‘Vertumnus II’, dating from Bitton Vicarage, Bristol, who took over conducting the ‘Monthly Packet Botanical Society’in the February 1884 issue, and ran it at least until January 1886.  His predecessor, who started the society in the June 1879 issue and dated from Preston Vicarage, Sandwich, was perhaps the Rt. Rev. Henry Lascelles Jenner or a member of his family.
References to this lady, resident in India, and inspired by Ann Carter Smith\'s work to give money to the poor of the East End, occur in letters to Carter Smith from 1861.

description: an unsatisfactory pupil of Mary Anne Dyson's, leaving (25 Feb 1854)

biography: She visited England in 1865-6 to raise funds for an Anglican cathedral and girls' school.
She may have been related to Dr. William England, perhaps his wife or his daughter-in-law.

He was the son of Dr. William England, and by 1899 had taken over the practice at 12 Southgate Street, Winchester. He married (1888) Catherine Harriette J. Ord. See Coleridge, Life 321n.: ‘Dr. England was the family physician. His son attended Miss Yonge in her last illness.’
See Coleridge, Life 321n.: ‘Dr. England was the family physician. His son attended Miss Yonge in her last illness.’ His wife’s name was Catherine.
She evidently knew the Dysons and Mary Coleridge.

description: eldest daughter of Edward Augustus Freeman
biography: She married (1878) Sir Arthur John Evans (1851-1941), archaeologist [ODNB Freeman and Evans]; she contributed to MP (1882). Either she, or possibly her sister Florence, took part in the Spider competitions under the name ‘Pisa’.

description: perhaps an official of the SPCK
biography: Another possibility is that the person mentioned in this letter to Susanna Warren of 3 November 1860 is the engraver Edmund Evans (1826-1905), but this seems less likely.
She married ([ODNB]

She married (1879) Charles Henry Seymour. She was one of the women who sailed to South Africa with Mary Anderson Morshead and Bishop Robert Gray in 1868, and the dedicatee of Morshead\'s Robert Gray; see her account there of work at Clewer.

title: 2nd Bt.
biography: He married (1848) Allison Callaway (d. 1907); he lived at Brambridge House, Hants by 1866. [ODNB; Dod 1876; PB 1952]
He was author of Occasional Thoughts (London E. Faithfull and Winchester Jacob and Johnson 1872), a volume of verse published by private subscription, probably sold in aid of the Winchester Hospital.

description: a schoolmistress at Winchester High School
biography: Perhaps a relation of E. W. Faithfull.
A protégé of Alexander Macmillan, formerly (1861 census) curator of Cambridge geological museum.
His sister married CMY’s cousin Edmund Anderson Morshead.
The translation of his novel was by FMY.
Probably the novelist of that name.
The person mentioned (15 Jan 1853) may be the same as the Mr Fielder, apparently a clergyman somewhere else, letter to him (1870) thanking for collection for Melanesia.
She was written to in Aug 1868 about Mary Anderson Morshead and ladies going to Cape Town.

CMY\'s neighbour Marion Finlaison (1834/5-1914) is described in Coleridge, [[otherbook:40]Life], 272, 280. She ran a small boarding-school in Otterbourne and acted as sub-editor of MP. Although Marion is what she wrote on the census forms, it appears she was actually baptised Catherine Jane. She was the daughter of William Finlaison (1789-1852), Captain RN (he was brother of the actuary and was on the Beagle, briefly also governor of Ascension I) and Mary Anne Ovenden. In 1861, calling herself Marion C. C [or J?]. Finlaison, she was living with her mother in the household of her sister Mary Isobell (1819-1900) and brother-in-law, the Rev. [[person:758]Henry Jenner] (1820-1898), Rector of Preston, Kent. Jenner was later made Bishop of Dunedin New Zealand (though rejected as too High) and Bishop of the Eglise Catholique Gallicane. Marion Finlaison acted as subeditor of the MP and ran a small boarding school in Otterbourne from late 1870s, probably successor of the school run by Mary Adams. She was evidently known by her family as Kate. She lived at Wingham between Preston and Otterbourne. [Not in PO Directory 1875, listed in White\'s Directory 1878; Finlaison letters; geocities.]

description: elementary schoolmaster in Otterbourne in the 1881 census
a friend of the Rev. William Bigg Wither
biography: He is mentioned (21 October 1844), and was perhaps engaged to be married.

He was made bishop in 1847, and attempted to bring about reunion with Rome. This was unpopular in Scotland and he was tried in 1860, Keble being present. He was a friend of Gladstone [J.B.Mowat, Bishop A.P. Forbes; ODNB]

Fifth and youngest daughter of William Forbes (1803-1891) of Medwyn and Mary Hume Archer Houblon (d.1896), niece of Alexander Penrose Forbes, Bishop of Brechin.  Her father was first cousin to Anne Mackenzie.  A Gosling as Thistle [2], and first cousin to Polypodium.  [Houblon Family;  LG 1952;  Faculty of Advocates]

Born in Scotland, he had a wife Maria Augusta 46 and niece Isabella Davidson 22 in 1851 census.  He had retired by 1861 and was living in Shirley Common Road, Millbrook parish. [Awdry, Heathcote;  White Directory of Hampshire 1859; 1851 census]
Perhaps the Mr Franke who wanted to translate one of CMYs novels
Friend and collaborator of CMY, father of Margaret and Florence Freeman. [ODNB]

description: daughter of E. A. Freeman, contributor to MP (1891-3)
biography: Either she, or possibly her sister Margaret, took part in the Spider competitions under the name ‘Pisa’. Unmarried in 1905, when she and her sister Helen were awarded a civil list pension in consideration of their father’s historical works. [The Times 22 June 1905]

She was the fourth daughter of William Frere (1775-1836), Master of Downing College, Cambridge. [LG 1952]  However, it is not clear whether or not the letter to Miss Frere (1875) who lived abroad, is addressed to her.
Third daughter of the Rev. Temple Frere (1781-1859); she was Augusta Frere’s first cousin.

biography: [ODNB]

railway engineer, son of the Ven. Richard Hurrell Froude

biography: He was honorary secretary of the Philological Society and the originator of the proposal for a New English Dictionary. He introduced CMY to Macmillan.

description: sister of Charlotte and Henrietta Fursdon.
biography: Fifth daughter of the Rev. Edward Fursdon, she was evidently not a member of the Gosling Society.

description: sister of Charlotte and Henrietta Fursdon
biography: Sixth daughter of the Rev. Edward Fursdon, she was evidently not a member of the Gosling Society. [LG 1952 Fursdon]
She was a Gosling as ‘Glow worm’, third daughter of the Rev. Edward Fursdon, and a contributor to MP (1893). [LG 1952 Fursdon]

description: sister of Charlotte and Henrietta Fursdon
biography: Eldest daughter of the Rev. Edward Fursdon, she was not a Gosling but probably contributed illustrations to The Barnacle [LG 1952 Fursdon]
He married (27 Feb 1838) his first cousin Harriet Grace Rodd [LG 1952 Fursdon of Fursdon, Rodd of Trebartha]

description: sister of the Rev. Edward Fursdon
biography: [wills index]
She was a Gosling as ‘Irene’ and second daughter of the Rev. Edward Fursdon. [LG 1952 Fursdon]
A Gosling as ‘Pixie’ 1870-1876, she was fourth daughter of the Rev. Edward Fursdon [LG 1952 Fursdon]
One of the women who sailed to South Africa with Mary Anderson Morshead and Bishop Robert Gray in 1868.

description: Dean of Ripon (1859) then Lincoln (1860) son of the Very Rev. Thomas Garnier, sr.
biography: [ODNB]

He became Dean of Winchester in 1840 and was also Rector of Bishopstoke, Hants.;  he resigned the rectory in 1868,  and the deanery about June 1872.  He married (1805) Mary Parry; and had four sons and four daus. [ODNB]

She was governess to the children of Philip Wynter,  president of St Johns College Oxford in 1861.  She was evidently daughter of the Rev. Richard Garnett (1789-1850), assistant keeper of printed books at the British Museum, and sister of Richard Garnett (1835-1906), keeper of printed books at the British Museum,  for she was staying with the latter in the 1871 census and still a governess.
Both these articles may be by Richard Garnett (1835-1906), keeper of printed books in the British Museum. [ODNB]
She was not related to Richard or Ellen Garnett.

She was known as Delia Garstin. For her connection with Cordelia Garstin (d.1791), who had been the first wife of FMY’s father, see Coleridge, Life, 33. She was the daughter of John Bradstreet Garstin of Wakering Hall, Essex and Mary Ketchum of New Brunswick.  She died in Exeter [LG 1871 Garstin]

title: 3rd Marquess of Sal
biography: He married (1857), Georgiana Caroline Alderson (1827-1899);  he was styled Lord Robert Cecil to 1865, then Viscount Cranborne until succeeding his father in 1868;  he served as Prime Minister 1885-6, 1886-7, 1887-92, 1895-1900, 1900-2. [ODNB]

title: Marchioness of Sal
description: wife of the 3rd Marquess of Salisbury

biography: She married (8 July 1839) the Rev. Alfred Gatty (1813-1903), Vicar of Ecclesfield; she was the mother of Juliana Horatia (Gatty) Ewing, and a contributor to MP (1857-69). Gatty’s Aunt Judy’s Tales (1859) and Aunt Judy’s Letters (1862) were made up of contributions to the MP from 1858 to 1865. \'Aunt Judy\' was there represented as an older sister telling stories to her younger brothers and sisters, and was based on Gatty’s daughter [[person:494]Juliana Horatia Gatty] (1841-1885), later Ewing, who herself began to contribute to the MP in 1861. In 1866 Gatty began to edit a periodical for George Bell called [[other:54]Aunt Judy’s Magazine] and most of the later fiction of both mother and daughter appeared there.

Elder daughter of the Rev. Charles Gaye, Rector of St. Matthews, Ipswich, she was author of fiction and non-fiction for children, including translations from Hungarian, sometimes as S.G. and sometimes as ‘A clergyman’s daughter’. She may well be the author of all contributions to MP signed S.G.. By the 1871 census she was an authoress living in London, Coleshill St., with an elderly ?aunt;  in 1891 and 1901 in London with brother Howard Gaye, architect, with no servant.

CMY’s bank account records the payment of £5 to Miss E. Gee on 10 April 1873, the only one to a person of this name. A story ‘What the Church Eagle Said’ appeared in MP (December 1872) 4. Evelyn Gee (b. Herts. 1843/4), daughter of the Rev. Richard Gee, Vicar of Abbots Langley and later of Windsor, who married (1880) Richard Rivington Holmes, librarian at Windsor Castle, seems a plausible candidate. He has an entry in ODNB, which states that she survived him.

Friend of Christina Rossetti, she also wrote as Gerda Fay, and was author of children's verse. She contributed to MP (1873), and probably also wrote the articles published as by C.M.Gemma (1862, 1864) [1851 census]
She married (1886) Julius Longard de Longgarde.  She was a prolific novelist, sometimes with her sister Emily, who lived in Galicia in the Austrian Empire.

description: novelist as E. Gerard, contributor to MP (1894)
biography: Sister of Dorothea Gerard, she married (1869) Miecislaus de Laszowski; she lived in Austria.

She was known as Blanche. Third daughter of Sir Thomas Crawley-Boevey 3rd Bt. she married (1 Aug 1839) William Gibbs (1790-1875) of Tyntesfield.  She was second cousin to CMY, her paternal grandfather being brother of WCY's mother.

title: 1st Lord Aldenham
biography: He was created (1896) 1st Lord Aldenham.  He married (1845) Louisa Anne Adams (d. 1895).  He was son of George Henry Gibbs (1785-1842), elder brother of William Gibbs of Tyntesfield.  His parents were first cousins, his mother being Caroline, sixth daughter of the Rev. Charles Crawley (1756-1849), Rector of Stowe Nine Churches, Northants., and Mary Gibbs (d.1819).  He was thus CMY’s second cousin. [ODNB, PB 1952]
Fourth son of William and Blanche Gibbs, he married (1882) Emily Anna Otter (d. 1928). [PB 1948]  He was CMY’s second cousin once removed.

He married (1839) Matilda Blanche Crawley-Boevey (1817/8-1887).  His aunt Mary Gibbs (d.1819) had married the Rev. Charles Crawley (1756-1849), brother of CMY’s paternal grandmother Catharina (Crawley) Yonge, the first of many marriages connecting the various families.  His wife was the granddaughter of Charles and Catharina Crawley’s eldest brother Sir Thomas Crawley-Boevey 2nd Bt. (1745-1818).
She sometimes wrote as A.G., and may be the author of earlier contributions to MP signed thus.

He married (1883) Emmeline Spratt.  He was a clerk in a City of London warehouse in the 1881 census.  He may or may not be the dissenting ‘clerk and of a station rather above, much given to good works’ to whom she was engaged in 1878.

description: contributor to MP (1876-9), novelist and writer on embroidery

title: Countess of Glasgow
biography: She was wife of the 6th Earl of Glasgow (d. 1890), the original of Harry in Catherine Sinclair’s Holiday House.

She wrote about Canterbury Cathedral in the \'Cathedral Sketches\' series in MP (1859). She was the author of nineteen stories and tracts published by the SPCK as ‘by the author of Hester Blake’ (a story published in 1855) and others as ‘by the author of The Chamois Hunter’ (a work of which there seems to be no COPAC record).
She was later (1865) Mrs Disney Leith.  She was a  niece of Lady Elinor Wodehouse and cousin of the poet Swinburne, who is said by some to have been in love with her.
Fifth dau of Sir William Gordon Cumming 2nd Bt. (1787-1854) and Eliza Campbell (d. 1842). [PB; Harvard Lib Cat]

description: contributor to MP, writer as Mrs J.E.H. Gordon
biography: She married (1878) James Edward Henry Gordon, electrical engineer (1852-1893) [His ODNB entry says her surname is  unknown, but the 1881 census has Gordon at 32 Elvaston Place Kensington with wife Alice M and his father-in-law Joseph E F Brandreth, rtd ICS, magistrate. Gordon’s mother was named Brandreth; perhaps they were cousins]

title: 1st Lord Glenelg
biography: He served as secretary of state for the colonies 1835-1839, notoriously lazy, he was created a peer in 1835.

The reference to a sculpture of John Coleridge Patteson in the letter refusing an article called ‘Second Fiddles’ suggests that it may have been addressed to the print seller of that name, although the identification is not certain.
He became Bishop of Cape Town in 1847. He married (1836) Sophia Wharton Myddleton. [Morshead, Robert Gray; ODNB]

description: wife of the Rt. Rev. Robert Gray, Bishop of Cape Town
biography: [ODNB]

description: writer on church music, contributor to MP (1881)

biography: She also contributed to Ladies at Work (London: Innes 1893).
She married (1852) Richard Jonas Greene. [PB 1948]

description: friend of Mary Adams and her aunt

biography: He was assistant editor from 1866; famous as the editor of the Dictionary of Music; he was knighted in 1883.

Youngest sister of Anne Mackenzie and of the Rt. Rev. Charles Frederick Mackenzie, she married in Natal (1861) the Rev. Charles Septimus Grubbe. (1830-1910), S. P. G. missionary at Maritzburg 1858-61 and Archdeacon of Maritzburg 1861-5.[Grubbe Family; LG Mackenzie]

He was SPG missionary at Maritzburg 1858-61 and Archdeacon of Maritzburg 1861-5. He married (1861) at Bishopstoke, Natal, Alice Mackenzie, youngest sister of CF Mackenzie [Genealogical Memoranda Relating to the Grubbe Family (1893)]

title: 6th Earl of Guilford
description: pluralist, son of the Bishop of Winchester
biography: He succeeded his distant cousin the fifth earl of Guilford in 1827. He was Master of St. Cross Hospital, Rector of St. Mary\'s, Southampton, and of Old Alresford, New Alresford and Medstead, mentioned by CMY (16 Jan 1854). He was a notorious pluralist and sparked the debates which gave rise to Trollope’s The Warden.

description: daughter of the Rev. Robert Guinness and Grace Harriet Butler
biography: [LG 1952 Guinness of Wootton Hall, Guinness Family]

biography: [LG 1952 Guinness of Wootton Hall, Guinness Family; 1891 census]

biography: She married (17 April 1866) the Rev. Robert Guinness (1841-1918),  [Guinness Family;  LG 1952 Guinness of Wootton Hall]

description: daughter of the Rev. Robert Guinness and Grace Harriet Butler
biography: [LG 1952 Guinness of Wootton Hall, Guinness Family]

biography: She married James Alfred Fort and had issue.  [LG 1952 Guinness of Wootton Hall, Guinness Family]
He gained his MD in 1846, was FRCP, was created a baronet 1872, and left £344,000 [ODNB]
He founded Malvern hydropathic establishment in the early 1840s, but was ruined by the Bravo case of 1876, which revealed he had had an affair with a patient.
He was private secretary to the 3rd Marquess of Salisbury 1816-73 and 1878-1903;  he was librarian at Hatfield House 1866-73 and 1878-1921.

description: Vicar of St. Barnabas, Pimlico, contributor to MP (1885-93)
biography: He was author of hymns, religious works and a study of D.G. Rossetti; he married (1866) Alice Blanche Gibbs, daughter of William Gibbs of Tyntesfield. [LG 1952]
Brother-in-law of Whistler, he was perhaps known to the Johns family.
He was editorial secretary to the SPCK, and published a biography of Bishop Mackenzie in 1870.

She was author of sanitary tracts and religious works. She was the daughter of the Rev. Canon Charles Pilkington and the wife of the Rev. John Thomas Hallett, Vicar of Bishop\'s Tachbrook, Warwickshire.

He married (1866) Louisa, second daughter of Lt- Col Edward Walter.  In the 1891 census he was living at Itchen Cottage, Itchen Abbas with his wife and daughters Georgina, 23, Edith, 22,  Dora E., 17, Gertrude, 14, Violet, 13, and son Frank, 11.  In the 1901 census he was living at Upcott, Bishops Hall, Somerset,  with his wife Louisa, 59, and daughters Elizabeth, 26, Gertrude, 24, Violet Amy, 22, and three servants. The probate of his will was obtained by Gertrude Louisa Charlotte Manley wife of Harry Lamont Manley.
She married (1901) Harry Lamont Manley, and she proved General Halliday’s will.
Sometimes called Dora. E. Halliday.

description: sister of Gertrude Walter and Frances (Walter) Yonge
biography: Daughter of Lt- Col Edward Walter, she married (1866) Francis Edward Halliday (1834-1911).  She was sister of Gertrude Walter, Frances Yonge and Mary (Walter) Woollcombe.  She had a large family of whom CMY most often mentions her daughter Georgina Frances (Halliday) Mansfield (b.1868/9) who was three in 1871. [India Office, Bombay Baptisms, 1871 census when they were staying at Medstead with cousins]
She also published a study of the Renaissance painter Gaudenzio Ferrari.
He was in charge of Otterbourne parish at the time of the 1881 census.
Daughter of the 2nd Marquess of Normanby, she married (1868) John Vivian Hampton (1835-1890), and is mentioned as a potential contributor in 1878.

title: Viscount Cranbrook,
biography: He was created (1878) Viscount Cranbrook and (1892) 1st Earl of Cranbrook. [ODNB]
Probably the German theologian Claus Harms (1778-1855).

She was a Gosling as ‘Albatross’ and left in 1863.  Daughter of Arthur Henry Dyke Acland Troyte (born Acland, 1811-1857) and Frances Williams (d. 1856), she married (1864) Leonard Harper, son of the Rt. Rev. Henry John Chitty Harper (1804-1893), first Bishop of Christchurch, New Zealand.  She had a double wedding with her sister Mary who married the Rev. Walter Hook [1851 census, PB 1948 Acland, LG 1952 Harper]

description: Bishop of Christchurch and primate of New Zealand

biography: Mentioned (24 Sept 1846).

description: step cousin of CMY, contributor to MP (1869, 1870)
biography: The only son of the Rev. Joseph H. Harris’s first marriage to Charlotte Collyer. She  died, probably in child birth in 1834 in Canada and Joseph remarried (1837) Jane Yonge, sister of Uncle Yonge, who had accompanied her sister Lady Seaton to Canada.  George Harris was born in Toronto and educated at Harrow and Exeter College Oxford (BA 1856, MA 1858)  He served as curate of Chipping Campden 1857-9, then Tor Mohun 1859-65;  he was Vicar of St Luke\'s, Torquay from 1865 until his death. He died at his parents\' house, Sorel, Torquay.  He married (London 1865) Percy [sic] Primrose (b. Quebec 1839/40) and had Edward Percy Harris (b.1866/7-?d.1872),  George Montagu Harris (b.1869) and Mary J Y Harris (b.1871), the latter the biographer of Frances Mary Peard. [Boase supp; 1871, 1901, 1881 census, information from Ian Yonge.]

description: daughter of the Rev. George Collyer Harris, biographer of Frances Mary Peard

biography: She married (1837, in Canada, where she had gone with the Seatons) the Rev. Joseph Hemington Harris (1799/1800-1881) D. D., incumbent of Torre, near Torquay, a widower with one son, the Rev. George Collyer Harris.
Described by CMY as 'a Plymouth man . .  a small man with a Jewish face and a nervous sensitive manner' [Coleridge, Life 100]

description: Vicar of Tor Mohun and Cockington
biography: He married, first, Charlotte Collyer. She died, probably in child birth in 1834 in Canada and H Joseph married (1837), also in Canada, Jane Yonge, CMY\'s father\'s first cousin. His only child, the Rev. George Collyer Harris was born of the first marriage. The Rev.Joseph Harris was educated at St Paul’s School and St John’s College, Cambridge, Fellow of Clare Coll, Cambridge 1824-9, priest 1825, principal of Upper Canada College 1829-38, curate of Cockington 1845-8, of Tor Mohun 1848- his death. Died at Sorel, Torquay, [obituary Guardian  29 June 1881, 913 ]

Daughter of the Venerable Canon Philip Jacob (1802/3-1884), rector from 1831 of Crawley with Hunton, north-west of Winchester, and canon and (from 1860) Archdeacon of Winchester, and his wife, Anna Sophia (1807?-1857), eldest daughter of the Hon. Gerard Thomas Noel, canon of Winchester. The parents were married in 1832. Edith, according to her brother Edgar 'was left in February, 1857, by the death of her mother . . . the eldest daughter of seven surviving children.'1 There were four sons and three daughters of the marriage; a son who went into the army; another son, who went into the navy, either one of whom may have been Eustace Wilberforce Jacob (b.?1834-9 July 1871), SPG missionary in South Africa; Isabel Margaret (b. 1840/1); Edgar (1844-1920); and Ernest Henry (1849-1894), MRCS. Their father had been brought up partly in Guernsey, and his father John Jacob (1765-1840) had published a history of the island. The family also had many connections with India. Edith lived at home, but became seriously ill early in 1868; her disease was described as 'congestion of the spine' and she spent most of the rest of her life in varying degrees of invalidism. During this first attack, according to her brother, she reflected on the contribution which invalids could make to the life of the Church. The result of this was a paper 'Thoughts on invalid life' published at the suggestion of CMY and reviewed by her in the Church Quarterly Review. This resulted in the foundation of the 'Society of Watchers and Workers', an organisation to which Edith Jacob devoted her energies for the rest of her life, and of whose privately printed journal, the Watchword, she was editor. This periodical ran 1880-1972; the BL has only odd volumes, but there is a complete run in Lambeth Palace Library. The BL's copies are bound with interesting rolls of members of the society; CMY is listed as a member of the executive committee. The activities of the society, which included support for homebound 'invalids of the cultured classes', enabling them to direct their energies in prayer and fundraising for charitable objects, are described in more detail in Kathleen Alice Orr, Letters (1907, 1909), a privately printed memoir of a deceased watcher with a memoir by Edith Jacob. The Watchers were especially keen on missions.

In the 1880s she began writing again, publishing three novels under the name Elizabeth Wormeley Latimer: Salvage (1880), My Wife and My Wife\'s Sister, 1881, and Princess Amélie: A Fragment of Autobiography (1883). In 1888 she published three translations from the French: History of the People of Israel, by Ernest Renan, and For Fifteen Years and Steel Hammer, both by Louis Ulbach and in 1890 George Sand’s Nanon. In the 1890s and early 1900s she published a series of books on the history of various European nations, and on the colonisation of Africa, three more translations and a final novel, Prince Incognito (1902).
